titel: The pope's dossier: the decretals of John XXII, 1317–1324
autor: Pope John XXII (Jacques Duèze, pope 1316–1334), five decretals collected among his Extravagantes under the title 'On the meaning of words' (De verborum significatione)
quelle: Corpus iuris canonici, ed. Emil Friedberg, vol. II: Decretalium collectiones (Leipzig: Tauchnitz, 1881), Extravagantes Ioannis XXII, tit. XIV De verborum significatione, c. 1–5, cols. 1220–1236. Read from the unaltered photomechanical reprint (Graz: Akademische Druck- und Verlagsanstalt, 1955), Internet Archive BD1141952; checked against the second reprint (Graz 1959). Public domain.
hinweis: The Latin is Friedberg's text. Two independent OCRs of the reprint were compared word by word, and every disagreement, every rare word form and every column carried was read against the page image; errors the two OCRs shared (concordandae for concordantiae, sea for sed, elavem for clavem, and letters lost at line ends) were corrected from the page. Friedberg's spelling (quum, diffinire), punctuation and brackets are kept; his footnote marks and apparatus are dropped, and the variants that matter are given in the notes (among them the manuscripts' 'Nicholas III' where his text prints 'Nicholas IV'). Quia nonnunquam, Ad conditorem canonum and Quum inter nonnullos are carried in full; Quorundam exigit and Quia quorundam in excerpts, the cuts marked […]. The medieval summaries (summaria) Friedberg prints before each chapter are translated in the notes, as later additions. The English is this site's working translation (CC0), rendering the legal terms for sense and giving the Latin in brackets where the argument turns on them.

sections.blurb: The pope's first word on the Franciscans: the Spirituals' short and patched habits, the granaries and cellars of the Community; the superiors decide, and the friars obey. 'Great is poverty; greater is integrity; obedience is the greatest good.' Excerpts.

units.orig: Quorundam exigit caecae scrupulositatis ambiguum, ac ipsorum quodammodo indocta scientia, (ne dixerimus, quod irreligiosa horum sit vana, et in hoc superstitiosa religio,) ut, dum suis mavult temere sub conscientiae velamento conceptibus, quam praelatorum ordinis sui cum obedientiae merito provide inhaerere sententiis, nos post praedecessorum nostrorum, et praesertim felicis recordationis Nicolai IV. ac piae memoriae Clementis V. Romanorum Pontificum super intellectu et observantia regulae ordinis fratrum Minorum declarationes salubriter editas, solidas quidem et claras, et lucidas multaque maturitate digestas, nostras Domino favente indubias ipsorum praedecessorum declarationibus declarationes adiungamus, sicque dies diei eructet verbum, et nox nocti scientiam manifestet, ne perperam paucorum dicti ordinis fratrum (quod absit) inscitia, recta ipsarum declarationum verba convertens in devium, illaque suis eis profecto contraria accommodans sensibus, ingrata Deo, superioribus contumax, praefato ordini detrahens, odiosa confratribus, unionem scindens, si valeat, reddatur, ac grave in populos scandalum allatura. […]
units.en: The blind scruple of certain men, and their somehow unlearned learning (not to say that their irreligious religion is vain, and in this superstitious), demand, since they would rather cling rashly to their own notions under the veil of conscience than wisely hold, with the merit of obedience, to the judgements of the superiors of their order, that after the declarations on the understanding and observance of the rule of the order of Friars Minor soundly issued by our predecessors, especially Nicholas IV of happy memory and Clement V of pious memory, Roman pontiffs (solid, clear and lucid declarations, digested with much deliberation), we should add, the Lord favouring us, our own undoubted declarations to theirs, so that day may pour forth speech to day and night show knowledge to night; lest the ignorance of a few friars of that order (God forbid) should wrongly turn the right words of those declarations aside, fit to their own sense what is contrary to it, and so become ungrateful to God, contumacious to their superiors, a detractor of the order, hateful to their brothers, a splitter of its unity if it can, and a cause of grave scandal among the peoples. […]
units.note: Dated at Avignon on 7 October 1317 (Friedberg's text breaks off with 'Nulli ergo etc. [1317.]'; the date is from a manuscript in his apparatus). The medieval summary printed before it: since the Friars Minor must wear poor clothing according to their rule, the pope leaves to the superiors what counts as poor, commands obedience to them under pain of excommunication, rebukes the friars who wore short, tight and novel habits of their own choosing, and says that obeying their superiors in this does not make them transgressors of the rule; the superiors may also decide whether the friars may have granaries and cellars; finally he exhorts them to obedience, which he places above poverty and chastity. Friedberg prints 'Nicolai IV.'; his manuscripts read III, and the declaration meant is Nicholas III's Exiit qui seminat (1279). The 'certain men' are the Spirituals of Provence and Tuscany, whom Clement V's Exivi de paradiso (1312) had tried to reconcile with the rest of the order. The psalm is Ps. 18 (19):3.

units.orig: […] Quin immo adeo huiusmodi adinventiones et quaestiones propria excrevere licentia, ut ex eisdem fratribus aliqui habitus propterea curtos, strictos, inusitatos et squalidos, novitate plenos ac dissidii non ignaros, quum a communitate ordinis discreparent, assumerent, nec eos ad ministrorum, custodum, guardianorum eorundem mandatum requisiti deponerent, nec alios, prout eiusdem ordinis communitas deferebat habitus, iuxta eorundem ministrorum, custodum et guardianorum arbitrium ducerent resumendos, dicentes, in hoc eorundem praelatorum suorum non parendum fore arbitrio, quum et suum sic despectum regularem et cruciformem assererent, ceterorum vero superfluum habitum irregularemque censerent, nec huic eorum opinioni praefati Clementis declarationem saepius repetitam obesse. […]
units.en: […] Indeed, such inventions and questions grew so far by their own licence that some of these friars took for this reason habits that were short, tight, unusual and squalid, full of novelty and not innocent of dissension, since they differed from the community of the order; and when required by the order of their ministers, custodians and guardians they would not put them off, nor would they consent to take again, at the discretion of those ministers, custodians and guardians, other habits such as the community of the order wore, saying that in this the judgement of their superiors was not to be obeyed, since they declared their own despised habit to be according to the rule and in the shape of the cross, and held the habit of the others to be superfluous and against the rule, and that Clement's often-repeated declaration did not stand in the way of this opinion of theirs. […]
units.note: The pope reports the Spirituals' case as it was argued before him and the cardinals by both sides; the general minister, Michael of Cesena, spoke 'for the community of the order'. Clement V had left the judgement of what was 'poor' clothing to the superiors, 'provided that they keep poverty in clothing': the Spirituals read the proviso as a limit on their superiors, the community as a formality.

units.orig: […] „nosque nihilominus praefatorum ministrorum, custodum et guardianorum iudicio praesentium auctoritate committimus, determinare videlicet, arbitrari atque praecipere, cuius longitudinis et latitudinis, grossitiei et subtilitatis, formae sive figurae, atque similium accidentium esse debeant tam habitus ipsorumque caputia quam interiores tunicae, quibus fratres omnes Minores dicti ordinis induuntur, ac insuper cuius quantaeque vilitatis indui eos ipsis vestimentis oporteat, et an in vestimentis huiusmodi secundum regulam et declarationes eorundem praedecessorum nostrorum et praefatas ordinis constitutiones reluceat asperitas, vilitas et paupertas, utrumne, quantum ad colorem, vilitatem, paupertatem quoque, ac cetera accidentia supra dicta fratres vestimentis induantur, ut debent.“ Super quibus eorundem ministrorum, custodum et guardianorum conscientias oneramus, statuentes et districte praecipiendo mandantes, quod in praedictis et his similibus eorum arbitrium, determinationem sive iudicium, generalis quidem in totius ordinis, provincialium vero in provinciarum ministrorum, ac custodum et guardianorum administrationibus, custodiis ac guardianiis, sive consimilibus ordinis memorati commissis eisdem fratres omnes et singuli sequi omnimode, illisque parere per omnia teneantur. […]
units.en: […] 'And we nevertheless, by the authority of these presents, commit to the judgement of the said ministers, custodians and guardians to determine, decide and command of what length and breadth, of what coarseness and fineness, of what shape or figure, and of what like accidents the habits with their hoods and the inner tunics of all the Friars Minor of the order must be; and moreover of what kind and how great a poverty of cloth they must be clothed in, and whether in such clothing, according to the rule, the declarations of our predecessors and the constitutions of the order, harshness, cheapness and poverty shine forth; and whether, as to colour, cheapness, poverty and the other accidents named above, the friars are clothed as they ought to be.' On these matters we burden the consciences of the ministers, custodians and guardians, and we ordain and strictly command that in these and similar matters all the friars, each and every one, be bound to follow in every way and obey in all things the judgement, determination or decision of the general minister in the whole order, of the provincial ministers in the provinces, and of the custodians and guardians in the custodies and houses entrusted to them. […]
units.note: The pope quotes his own decision within the decretal (the words between the marks). 'Burdening their consciences' makes the superiors answerable before God for the judgement, and so relieves the friars who obey them.

units.orig: […] nos de praedictorum fratrum nostrorum consilio eorundem ministrorum et custodum sub eadem forma iudicio praesentium auctoritate committimus, determinare videlicet, arbitrari atque praecipere eo casu, qualiter, ubi, et quando, et quoties granum, panem et vinum pro vitae fratrum necessariis fratres ipsi quaerere debeant, conservare sive reponere, etiamsi reponenda sint in praedictis granariis et cellariis conservanda, statuentes et districte praecipiendo mandantes, quod in praedictis et his similibus eorundem arbitrium, determinationem sive iudicium generalis quidem in totius, provincialium vero in provinciarum, ministrorum ac custodum simul et separatim administrationibus et custodiis ordinis memorati commissis eisdem, cum guardiani tamen (ut supra praedicitur) et duorum de conventu loci discretorum sacerdotum et antiquorum in ordine fratrum consilio et assensu, fratres omnes et singuli obsequi omnimode, illisque parere per omnia teneantur. […]
units.en: […] on the advice of our brothers we commit, by the authority of these presents and in the same form, to the judgement of those ministers and custodians to determine, decide and command in that case how, where, when and how often the friars must seek grain, bread and wine for the necessities of their life, and keep or store them, even if they are to be stored and kept in the said granaries and cellars; and we ordain and strictly command that in these and similar matters all the friars, each and every one, be bound to follow in every way and obey in all things the judgement, determination or decision of the general minister in the whole order, and of the provincial ministers and custodians, together or separately, in the provinces and custodies entrusted to them (with the advice and consent, as said above, of the guardian and two discreet priests of the house, of long standing in the order). […]
units.note: Clement V had allowed granaries and cellars only where it was 'very credible from experience' that the friars could not otherwise find the necessities of life. The Spirituals held that storing provisions broke the rule; here the decision passes to the superiors.

units.orig: […] Ideoque omnes et singulos fratres ante dicti ordinis Minorum, qui strictos, curtos et difformes habitus ab ipsius generalis ministri et aliorum de dicta communitate habitu coram nobis et fratribus nostris et aliis in Romana curia detulerunt vel deferunt, monemus et hortamur in Domino, eis nihilominus in virtute sanctae obedientiae et sub excommunicationis poena per apostolica scripta mandantes, quatenus ad mandatum ipsius generalis deponant quos deferunt habitus, et aliis iuxta eiusdem generalis arbitrium, determinationem sive iudicium (ut supra praedicitur) induantur, ipsique generali in omnibus istis et aliis, et per omnia secundum beati Francisci regulam et praedictas praedecessorum nostrorum declarationes, concessiones et commissiones in ipsis declarationibus comprehensas, et nostras contentas in praesentibus humiliter obediant, pareant et intendant, non obstantibus quibuscunque privilegiis, indulgentiis, literis, libertatibus, immunitatibus vel exemptionibus, eis vel alicui ipsorum a praefato Clemente concessis, vel appellationibus ab eis vel ipsorum aliquo ad sedem apostolicam interiectis, quae, in quantum possent derogare praesentibus, viribus vacuamus. Religio namque perimitur, si a meritoria subditi obedientia subtrahantur. Magna quidem paupertas, sed maior integritas bonum est, obedientia maximum, si custodiatur illaesa. Nam prima rebus, secunda carni, tertia vero menti dominatur et animo, quos velut effrenes et liberos ditioni alterius humilis iugo propriae voluntatis adstringit. […]
units.en: […] Therefore all and each of the friars of the said order of Minors who have worn and still wear, before us, our brothers and others in the Roman curia, tight, short and deformed habits, differing from the habit of the general minister and the others of the community, we warn and exhort in the Lord, and nonetheless command them by apostolic letters in virtue of holy obedience and under pain of excommunication, to put off the habits they wear at the command of the general, and put on others at his discretion, determination or judgement (as said above), and humbly to obey, submit to and attend to the general in these and all other things, entirely according to the rule of blessed Francis, the declarations, concessions and commissions of our predecessors contained in those declarations, and our own contained in these presents; notwithstanding any privileges, indulgences, letters, liberties, immunities or exemptions granted to them or any of them by Clement, or any appeals lodged by them or any of them to the apostolic see, which we deprive of force in so far as they could derogate from these presents. For religious life is destroyed if subjects withdraw from meritorious obedience. Great is poverty; greater is integrity; obedience is the greatest good, if it is kept unharmed. For the first rules over things, the second over the flesh, but the third over the mind and the spirit, which it binds, as if unbridled and free, under the rule of another by the humble yoke of one's own will. […]
units.note: The three vows of religious life: poverty, chastity ('integrity') and obedience. The sentence 'Magna quidem paupertas…' became the watchword of the dispute's first phase: in 1317 the question was not what Christ owned but whom a friar must obey. Four Spiritual friars who refused were burned at Marseille in May 1318. The decretal continues with an appeal to return in love, in the words of the Song of Songs, which is not carried here.

sections.blurb: Nicholas III had forbidden anyone, on pain of excommunication, to gloss or dispute his decretal Exiit qui seminat. John XXII suspends the ban: 'hidden truth is often opened by arguments and discussions'. The question of Christ's poverty is open.

units.orig: Quia nonnunquam, quod coniectura profuturum credidit, subsequens experientia nocivum ostendit: non debet reprehensibile iudicari, si canonum conditor canones a se vel suis praedecessoribus editos, vel aliqua in eisdem contenta canonibus revocare, modicare vel suspendere studeat, si ea obesse potius viderit quam prodesse.
units.en: Since what conjecture has sometimes believed would be useful, later experience shows to be harmful, it should not be judged reprehensible if the maker of the canons takes care to revoke, modify or suspend canons issued by himself or his predecessors, or anything contained in them, if he sees that they do more harm than good.
units.note: Dated at Avignon, 26 March 1322. The medieval summary printed before it: those who gloss the decretal Exiit qui seminat incur excommunication by the act itself, notwithstanding any privileges; the pope suspends that excommunication at the pleasure of the apostolic see, and by the suspension does not mean to give occasion for speaking against the Friars Minor. The opening sentence is a principle John XXII repeats nine months later, almost word for word, at the head of Ad conditorem canonum (Decr. Conditorem [1]).

units.titel: Exiit was not to be glossed
units.orig: Sane, dudum felicis recordationis Nicolaus Papa IV. praedecessor noster quandam constitutionem declarativam, quae incipit: „Exiit,“ super regula dilectorum filiorum fratrum ordinis Minorum, quam beatus Franciscus almus confessor instituit, promulgavit, sub certis poenis arctius interdicens, ne concordantiae, contrarietates, seu adversae vel diversae opiniones ab ipsius constitutionis lectoribus seu expositoribus aliquatenus inducantur, nec super constitutione glossae fiant ab aliquibus, nisi forsan, per quas verbum vel sensus ipsius, vel ipsa constitutio quasi grammaticaliter et ad literam exponatur, nec intellectus ipsius per legentem distorqueatur ad aliud, quam constitutionis eiusdem litera ipsa sonat; glossantes autem in scriptis constitutionem eandem aliter, quam superius est expressum, facientes quoque commenta, scripturas seu libros, et ex certa scientia et deliberatione determinantes in scholis seu praedicantes contra contenta in constitutione praedicta, vel aliqua seu aliquod praedictorum, (non obstantibus aliquibus privilegiis seu indulgentiis aut literis apostolicis, quibuscunque personis, dignitatibus, ordinibus, aut locis religiosis vel saecularibus generaliter vel singulariter sub quacunque forma vel expressione verborum concessis, quae noluit aliquibus in praedictis quomodolibet suffragari,) ipso facto excommunicationis sententiae voluit subiacere.
units.en: Pope Nicholas IV of happy memory, our predecessor, formerly promulgated a declaratory constitution beginning 'Exiit' on the rule of our beloved sons the friars of the order of Minors, which blessed Francis the gracious confessor founded; and under certain penalties he strictly forbade that any concordances, contradictions, or contrary or differing opinions be brought in by the readers or expositors of that constitution, and that glosses be made on it by anyone, except perhaps such as expound its words or sense, or the constitution itself, as it were grammatically and to the letter, and that its meaning be twisted by a reader to anything other than what the letter of the constitution itself says; and he willed that those who glossed the constitution in writing otherwise than stated above, or made commentaries, writings or books, or knowingly and deliberately determined in the schools or preached against what is contained in it, or any of it (notwithstanding any privileges, indulgences or apostolic letters granted to any persons, dignities, orders, or religious or secular places, generally or singly, in whatever form or expression of words, which he would not have avail anyone in this at all), should fall by the act itself under sentence of excommunication.
units.note: Friedberg prints 'Nicolaus Papa IV.'; his manuscripts read III. Exiit qui seminat is Nicholas III's (14 August 1279), and its ban on glossing was the order's shield: whoever questioned the friars' poverty questioned a papal decretal, and was excommunicated for it. The ban itself: Exiit [8].

units.orig: Nos autem, attendentes, quod argumentis frequenter et collationibus latens veritas aperitur, quodque sub eadem litera saepe latet multiplex intellectus, nec non esse difficile, volentibus constitutionem praedictam perfecte legere ac intelligere, poenas adiectas in constitutione huiusmodi devitare, viam veritatis aperire volentes, et periculis, quae ex praedictis possent literatae personae, praecipue scholasticae, incurrere, salubriter obviare, praesertim quum de novo suborta sint aliqua dubia, circa quae posset periclitari veritas, erroribus via pandi, nisi liceret conferre super contentis in constitutione huiusmodi et disputare, prohibitiones et poenas praedictas, tam latas quam comminatas, et earum effectus in fratrum nostrorum ac multorum archiepiscoporum, episcoporum et aliorum praelatorum, nec non multorum professorum utriusque iuris, et multorum sacrae theologiae magistrorum praesentia, dum consistorium teneremus, auctoritate apostolica duximus usque ad sedis apostolicae beneplacitum suspendendas. Per suspensionem autem huiusmodi nequaquam licentiam cuiquam intendimus impertiri, quod contra fratrum regulam praedictorum dogmatizare, scribere seu determinare, praedicare seu prave loqui liceat publice vel occulte; quin immo haec omnibus et singulis auctoritate praedicta districtius inhibemus. Ne autem in posterum praemissarum prohibitionum et poenarum suspensio in dubium revocari valeat, aut alicui propter defectum probationis impingi, quod velut transgressor prohibitionum ipsarum in poenam seu poenas inciderit ante dictas: nos, volentes super hoc de opportuno remedio providere, chartas seu membranas, suspensionem continentes eandem, appendi seu affigi in maioris ecclesiae Avinionensis ostiis seu superliminaribus faciemus, quae suspensionem praedictam suo quasi sonoro praeconio et patenti iudicio publicabunt. Dat. Avin. VII. Kal. April. Ao. VI. [1322.]
units.en: We, however, considering that hidden truth is often opened by arguments and discussions, that under the same letter a manifold meaning often lies hidden, and that it is difficult for those who wish to read and understand that constitution perfectly to avoid the penalties it adds; wishing to open the way of truth and to meet in good time the dangers that literate persons, especially scholars, could incur from it, above all since some doubts have newly arisen through which the truth could be endangered and a way opened to errors unless it were permitted to confer and dispute on what the constitution contains: we have suspended, by apostolic authority, until the pleasure of the apostolic see, those prohibitions and penalties, both inflicted and threatened, and their effects, in the presence of our brothers and of many archbishops, bishops and other prelates, and of many professors of both laws and many masters of sacred theology, while we held consistory. By this suspension, however, we by no means intend to give anyone licence to dogmatize, write or determine, preach or speak ill, publicly or in secret, against the rule of the said friars; on the contrary, we strictly forbid this to each and all by the same authority. And lest the suspension of the said prohibitions and penalties could in future be called in doubt, or anyone be charged for lack of proof with having incurred those penalties as a transgressor of the prohibitions, we, wishing to provide a fitting remedy, will have sheets or parchments containing the suspension hung or fixed on the doors or lintels of the cathedral church of Avignon, which will publish it as by a loud herald and an open judgement. Given at Avignon, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth year [1322].
units.note: The 'doubts newly arisen' are the Narbonne case of 1321, in which a Beguin's assertion that Christ and the apostles owned nothing, individually or in common, was declared heretical by the inquisitor and defended by a Franciscan lector, and the matter came to the pope. Suspending the ban made the question disputable; within three months the Franciscan general chapter at Perugia answered it.

sections.blurb: The legal core of the dispute. Since 1279 the Roman Church had owned what the friars used. John XXII calls that ownership 'verbal, bare and enigmatic': no one can use an egg, a cheese or a crust of bread without owning it, an act of use cannot be 'had', and a use without right would be unjust. The Church renounces the ownership and abolishes the procurators.

units.titel: The maker of the canons, and Nicholas' ordinance
units.orig: Ad conditorem canonum non est dubium pertinere, quum statuta, a se vel praedecessoribus suis edita obesse percipit potius quam prodesse, ne ulterius obesse valeant providere. Dudum siquidem felicis recordationis Nicolaus IV. praedecessor noster, attente prospiciens in almi confessoris, beati videlicet Francisci, regula contineri, quod nihil sibi approprient, neque domum, neque locum, neque rem aliquam aliam sui ordinis professores, ac considerans diligenter, quod per piae recordationis Gregorii Papae IX. et nonnullos alios praedecessores eiusdem fuerat declaratum, hoc debere servari tam in speciali quam in communi, nec non et consideranter attendens, nonnullos fratribus ipsis detrahere, impingentes eisdem, quod regulam et declarationes huiusmodi non observabant, pieque considerans, ora contra praemissos fratres oblatrantium claudere, ac professorum ipsorum conscientiis providere, inter alia ordinavit et sanxit, omnium utensilium et librorum, rerumque mobilium, et praesentium et etiam futurarum, ecclesiarum quoque et oratoriorum ac coemeteriorum, tam praesentium quam etiam futurorum, nec non et aliarum emptarum, et eleemosynis divinis oblatarum seu concessarum dictis fratribus, (in quibus tamen offerentes seu concedentes ipsa nihil in ipsis sibi ducerent reservandum,) proprietatem et dominium plene ac libere ad se et Romanam ecclesiam pertinere, ipsa in se recipiens ac ante dictam ecclesiam, simplici usu facti duntaxat in rebus et bonis huiusmodi reservato fratribus ante dictis.
units.en: It undoubtedly belongs to the maker of the canons, when he perceives that statutes issued by himself or his predecessors do more harm than good, to see that they do no further harm. Our predecessor Nicholas IV of happy memory, attentively considering that the rule of the gracious confessor, blessed Francis, contains that its professors shall appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house, nor place, nor anything else; and diligently considering that it had been declared by Pope Gregory IX of pious memory and several other of his predecessors that this was to be kept both individually and in common (tam in speciali quam in communi); and considering also that some were disparaging the friars, charging them with not observing the rule and such declarations; and piously wishing to shut the mouths of those who barked against the friars and to provide for the consciences of the professors, ordained and decreed among other things that the property and ownership (proprietatem et dominium) of all utensils and books, and of movable goods present and future, of churches, oratories and cemeteries present and future, and of other goods bought, or offered or granted to the friars by divine alms (in which, however, those offering or granting reserved nothing for themselves), belonged fully and freely to himself and the Roman Church; he took them into his own ownership and that of the said Church, reserving to the friars only the simple use of fact (simplici usu facti) in such things and goods.
units.note: Dated 8 December 1322. The medieval summary printed before it: the pope refutes the ownership of the things that came to the Friars Minor, retained by the Roman Church with the simple use of fact reserved to the friars in Exiit qui seminat, proving by many reasons that they cannot have a simple use of fact in anything, and decrees that henceforth the Roman Church shall have no right and no ownership in such things offered to them; 'this extravagant is very juridical and subtle in many places, above all where it proves that simple use cannot exist in things consumed by use'. Friedberg again prints 'Nicolaus IV.' where his manuscripts read III. The text of the Extravagantes is generally taken to be the revised version that John XXII issued in January 1323, after the Franciscan protest in consistory, under the date of the first. Nicholas III's ordinance is carried in Exiit [6].

units.orig: Et quia nonnunquam libros et alia mobilia supra dicta vendi expedit seu etiam commutari: fratribus ipsis in eadem ordinatione concessit, ut res ipsas cum rebus aliis, quarum usum habere licet ipsis fratribus, (dummodo generalis et provincialium ministrorum coniunctim vel divisim auctoritas intercederet,) possent libere commutare. Sed et quia fratribus ipsis pecuniam per se vel per alium recipere ipsorum regula districtius interdicit: voluit et concessit, quod, si vendi contingeret res mobiles ante dictas pretio aestimato, quod huiusmodi pretium per procuratorem deberet recipi, a praefata sede, vel cardinali gubernatore eiusdem ordinis deputandum, per procuratorem eundem in rem licitam, cuius usus esset permissus eiusdem ordinis fratribus, expendendum, hoc adiecto, quod possent de vilibus rebus mobilibus vel parum valentibus fratres ipsi pietatis seu devotionis intuitu, vel pro alia honesta causa et rationabili, (obtenta tamen super hoc superiorum suorum licentia,) intra vel extra dictum ordinem ordinare.
units.en: And since it is sometimes expedient that books and the other movables mentioned be sold or exchanged, he granted the friars in the same ordinance that they might freely exchange these things for other things whose use the friars may have (provided the authority of the general and the provincial ministers, jointly or severally, intervened). And since their rule strictly forbids the friars to receive money themselves or through another, he willed and granted that, if movable goods came to be sold at an assessed price, the price should be received by a procurator, to be appointed by the apostolic see or by the cardinal governor of the order, and spent by that same procurator on some lawful thing whose use was permitted to the friars; adding that the friars might, from motives of piety or devotion, or for another honest and reasonable cause (with the leave of their superiors), dispose of cheap movables or things of little value within or outside the order.
units.note: The procurator was the legal device that let a propertyless order live in a world of money: he held, sold and litigated in the name of the Roman Church, so that the friars touched neither coin nor title.

units.titel: It did not make them more perfect
units.orig: Quanquam autem pia consideratione motus praedecessor noster ordinavit supra dicta, illa dicto ordini existimans profutura: ipsa tamen attento modo utendi fratrum ipsorum ac dictae ecclesiae subsecuta patientia circa ipsum non profuisse, sed potius tam ipsis fratribus quam multis aliis obfuisse, subsequens magistra rerum experientia noscitur declarasse. Ipsis quidem fratribus, quantum ad statum perfectionis, nequaquam profuit reservatio dominii supra dicta. Quum enim perfectio vitae Christianae principaliter et essentialiter in caritate consistat, quae ab Apostolo perfectionis vinculum dicitur, et quae unit seu iungit aliqualiter in via hominem suo fini, ad quam per contemptum bonorum temporalium et ipsorum expropriationem via disponitur, per hoc praecipue, quod sollicitudo, quam temporalia in acquirendo, conservando et dispensando exigunt, quae plerumque ab actu caritatis retrahit, amputetur: restat, quod, si sollicitudo eadem post expropriationem huiusmodi, quae ante ipsam inerat, perseveret, ad perfectionem huiusmodi talis expropriatio valeat nihil conferre. Constat autem, quod post ordinationem praedictam non fuerint in acquirendis ac conservandis bonis praedictis in iudicio et extra minus solliciti, quam ante illam fuerant fratres ipsi, quanquam sint religiosi mendicantes alii, habentes aliqua in communi.
units.en: Although our predecessor ordained these things moved by a pious consideration, thinking them useful to the order, experience, the teacher of things, has since shown that, given the friars' way of using and the Church's forbearance with it, they have not been useful, but rather harmful both to the friars and to many others. To the friars, in the state of perfection, the reservation of ownership was no use at all. For since the perfection of the Christian life consists principally and essentially in charity, which the Apostle calls the bond of perfection, and which in some way unites or joins a man on his way to his end, and since the way to it is prepared by contempt of temporal goods and by giving up their ownership, chiefly because the anxiety that temporal things demand in acquiring, keeping and dispensing, which often draws a man away from the act of charity, is cut off: it follows that, if the same anxiety that was there before continues after the giving up of ownership, such an expropriation can contribute nothing to that perfection. And it is established that after the said ordinance the friars were no less anxious, in court and out of it, in acquiring and keeping those goods than they had been before, although there are other mendicant religious who have some things in common.
units.note: 'The bond of perfection': Col. 3:14. The argument turns the friars' own ideal against them: poverty is a means to charity, and a poverty that leaves the anxiety about things intact is not poverty. 'Other mendicant religious … in common': the Dominicans and the other mendicant orders owned property in common, and the Franciscans claimed a higher poverty than theirs.

units.orig: Adhuc nec utique profuit dictis fratribus ordinatio supra dicta, quantum ad hoc, quod propter carentiam talis proprii se pauperiores dicere valeant, quam si res ipsas cum illo, (quo carere se dicunt,) dominio obtinerent. Licet etiam praedecessor noster praedictus dominium earum rerum, quae ipsis fratribus offerri seu conferri, aut alias obvenire contigerit, quarum tamen usum facti duntaxat habere licet ordini vel fratribus ante dictis, usu facti simplici praedictis fratribus reservato, in se Romanamque ecclesiam recipiendum duxerit, ac libere pertinere decreverit, ut superius est expressum: attento tamen ipsorum fratrum utendi modo, et eius effectu, ac patientia circa modum ipsum Romanae ecclesiae subsecuta, non ipse usus fratrum dici debet, sed potius Romanae ecclesiae dominium esse simplex. Quis enim simplicem usuarium dicere poterit, cui rem usuariam licet permutare, vendere ac donare? Procul dubio haec naturae repugnare noscuntur, nec ad usuarium pertinere, quae tamen de rebus mobilibus ante dictis faciunt fratres ipsi. Quod autem dominium Romanae ecclesiae reservatum simplex censeri debeat, ex hoc patet, quod ex illo nullum eidem ecclesiae temporale obvenit hactenus commodum, nec speratur, quod obvenire debeat in futurum, quum nec intentio reservantis, nec fratrum ipsorum fuerit, quod ad quemcunque alium, quam ad fratres, dictarum rerum perveniret compendium, quod procul dubio modus utendi fratrum ipsorum, et Romanae ecclesiae subsecuta patientia evidenter declaravit. Et quod talis intentio fuerit ordinantis, et ex hoc patet, quod illarum rerum sibi et ecclesiae Romanae dominium duntaxat retinuit, quarum usum facti liceret habere ordini vel fratribus ante dictis. Talis autem dominii carentia re in praesenti, ac spe in futurum omni modo denudati, quoad paupertatem temporalem, quam altiorem prae mendicantibus aliis in communi habentibus sibi vindicant dicti fratres, pauperiorem non efficit non habentem.
units.en: Nor did the ordinance benefit the friars in this, that for lack of such property they could call themselves poorer than if they held the things with that ownership which they say they lack. For although our predecessor decided to take into his own ownership and that of the Roman Church the ownership of the things offered, granted or otherwise coming to the friars, whose use of fact alone the order or the friars may have, reserving the simple use of fact to the friars, and decreed that it belonged to it freely, as said above: yet, considering the friars' way of using, and its effect, and the Roman Church's forbearance with that way, it is not the use of the friars that should be called simple, but rather the ownership of the Roman Church. For who can call a man a simple user who may exchange, sell and give away the thing he uses? Beyond doubt these things are known to be contrary to the nature of use and not to belong to a user; and yet the friars do them with the said movables. That the ownership reserved to the Roman Church must be called simple is clear from this: no temporal benefit has come to that Church from it so far, nor is any hoped for in future, since it was the intention neither of the one who reserved it nor of the friars that the profit of those things should come to anyone but the friars; which the friars' way of using and the Church's forbearance have beyond doubt made evident. And that this was the intention of the one who ordained it is also clear from this, that he retained for himself and the Roman Church the ownership only of those things whose use of fact the order or the friars might have. Lack of such ownership, stripped in every way of any thing at present and any hope for the future, does not make the one who lacks it poorer as to temporal poverty, which the friars claim for themselves as higher than that of the other mendicants who have things in common.
units.note: The heart of the pope's case: the friars' 'simple use' and the Church's 'bare ownership' were a legal fiction. The friars had the whole benefit of the things; the Church had only the name of owner, and with it the lawsuits (Decr. Conditorem [10]).

units.titel: One egg, one cheese, one crust of bread
units.orig: Quod autem quoad res, quae usu consumuntur, non sint censendi usuarii fratres ipsi, ex sequentibus liquet satis. Dicere siquidem, quod in talibus rebus usus iuris vel facti, separatus a proprietate rei seu dominio, possit constitui, repugnat iuri, et obviat rationi, nec praedecessoris nostri praedicta fuisse videtur intentio, Romanae ecclesiae talium bonorum dominium reservare. Quis enim sanae mentis credere poterit, quod intentio fuerit tanti patris, unius ovi, seu casei, aut frusti panis, et aliorum usu consumptibilium, quae saepe fratribus ipsis ad consumendum e vestigio conferuntur, dominium Romanae ecclesiae, et usum fratribus retinere? Profecto probabile non videtur: praesertim quum illorum bonorum duntaxat dominium praefatae ecclesiae reservaverit, quorum simplex usus facti pertinere potest ad fratres dicti ordinis. Quod nequaquam potest in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri, in quibus nec ius utendi, nec usus facti, separata a rei proprietate seu dominio, possunt constitui vel haberi. Et quod de talibus rebus non intellexerit, evidenter ostendit, dum respondet legi, dicenti, non posse usumfructum a dominio perpetuo separari, ne dominium dominis, semper abscendente usu, inutile redderetur. Quae quidem lex de rebus illis intelligitur, quarum penes unum usus rei, et penes alium dominium possit, licet inutile, remanere; quod nequaquam in rebus usu consumptibilibus potest esse, quum in illis per usum vel abusum usuarii substantia talis rei esse desinat, et per consequens proprietas etiam inutilis non subsistat.
units.en: That in things consumed by use the friars are not to be considered users follows clearly enough from what follows. To say that in such things a use, of right or of fact, separated from the property or ownership of the thing, can be constituted is contrary to law and against reason; nor does it seem to have been our predecessor's intention to reserve to the Roman Church the ownership of such goods. For who of sound mind can believe that it was the intention of so great a father to retain for the Roman Church the ownership of one egg, or a cheese, or a crust of bread, and of other things consumed by use, which are often given to the friars to be consumed on the spot, and to leave the friars the use? Surely it does not seem probable; above all since he reserved to the Church the ownership only of those goods whose simple use of fact can belong to the friars of the order. This can by no means be found in things consumed by use, in which neither the right of using nor the use of fact, separated from the property or ownership of the thing, can be constituted or had. And that he did not mean such things he shows plainly when he answers the law which says that usufruct cannot be separated from ownership for ever, lest ownership become useless to the owners if the use were always absent. That law is understood of those things whose use can remain with one person and whose ownership, though useless, can remain with another; which can by no means be the case with things consumed by use, since in them the substance of the thing ceases to exist through the use or 'abuse' of the user, and in consequence not even a useless property remains.
units.note: The 'law' is the Roman-law rule that usufruct may not be separated from ownership for ever (Inst. 2.4.1), which Exiit qui seminat had answered. Roman law treated things consumed by use (money, grain, wine) apart: they can only be lent by transferring ownership (mutuum), and a 'usufruct' of them is a 'quasi-usufruct' that makes the user owner. John XXII applies that rule to the friars' bread, against Nicholas III's answer to it (Exiit [5]).

units.titel: Usufruct, use, the right of using
units.orig: Quum enim ususfructus, prout est in re constitutus, qui servitus dicitur personalis, et pro quo reales competunt actiones, nihil sit aliud, quam ius utendi, nec usus, qui etiam personalis est servitus, sit aliud, quam ius tantum utendi rebus alienis, salva rei substantia, id est, ius percipiendi fructus et utilitatem aliam in totum vel pro parte suo nomine, qui possunt ex re, in qua ususfructus seu usus constituitur, provenire, propter quod proprietas reputatur inutilis, a qua perpetuo abscedit ususfructus, seu usus constitutus rebus, ex quibus ipsis stantibus usufructuario seu usuario nulla possit utilitas provenire: patet, quod ad hoc, quod talis ususfructus vel usus in re aliqua constitui valeat, requiritur, quod ex re illa possint fructus vel utilitas salva ipsius rei substantia ad fructuarium vel usuarium pervenire. Quodsi nulla ad ipsos posset ex re ipsa utilitas salva rei substantia pervenire, quales res constat esse usu consumptibiles: nequaquam posset in rebus ipsis cuiquam ususfructus vel usus constitui, vel a quoquam haberi. Adhuc nec ius utendi, quod nec est ius in re, nec servitus personalis, sed mere ius personale, pro quo reales actiones non competunt, in rebus talibus vel rebus ipsis utendi potest constitui vel haberi, quum et ius tale exigat, quod ex re ipsa, quae ad utendum conceditur, tali modo ad usuarium pervenire posset utilitas aliqua, ac cum usu permanere usuarii substantia salva rei, quod nequaquam potest, (sicut ad sensum potest percipi,) in rebus usu consumptibilibus reperiri. Rursus nec simplex usus, qui nec est servitus, nec pro illo competit ius utendi, in talibus rebus potest constitui vel haberi. Quum enim uti re aliqua nihil sit aliud proprie, quam fructus rei sive utilitatem aliam in solidum vel pro parte recipere, qui ex ea possunt salva rei substantia provenire: restat, quod re illa uti quis nequeat, ex qua eius salva substantia nulla sibi provenire potest utilitas, quales res usu consumptibiles esse constat. Ex quibus patet, quod nec usus, qui est servitus personalis, nec ius utendi, quod non est servitus, sed mere ius personale, nec actus ipse utendi sine iure aliquo possunt in rebus usu consumptibilibus constitui vel haberi, quum quodlibet praemissorum exigat, quod ex re ipsa salva rei substantia possit habenti ius utendi, seu utenti ex re ipsa utilitas aliqua provenire, quod utique in rebus nequit usu consumptibilibus reperiri.
units.en: For since usufruct, as constituted in a thing, which is called a personal servitude and for which real actions lie, is nothing but a right of using; and use, which is also a personal servitude, is nothing but a right only of using the things of another, their substance being preserved, that is, a right of taking in whole or in part, in one's own name, the fruits and other benefit that can come from the thing in which the usufruct or use is constituted (for which reason the property from which a usufruct is for ever separated is thought useless); and since a usufruct or use constituted in things from which, while they remain, no benefit could come to the usufructuary or user, would be none: it is clear that, for a usufruct or use to be constituted in anything, it is required that fruits or benefit can come from that thing to the usufructuary or user while its substance is preserved. But if no benefit could come to them from the thing while its substance is preserved, as is the case with things consumed by use, no usufruct or use could be constituted for anyone in them, or be had by anyone. Further, neither can a right of using, which is neither a right in a thing nor a personal servitude, but merely a personal right, for which no real actions lie, be constituted or had in such things, since such a right too requires that some benefit could come to the user from the thing granted for use in such a way that its substance remains with the use; which can by no means be found (as the senses can perceive) in things consumed by use. Again, neither can a simple use, which is not a servitude and for which no right of using lies, be constituted or had in such things. For since to use a thing is properly nothing but to receive, in whole or in part, the fruits or other benefit of the thing that can come from it while its substance is preserved, it follows that no one can use a thing from which, its substance preserved, no benefit can come to him; and such are the things consumed by use. From which it is clear that neither use, which is a personal servitude, nor the right of using, which is not a servitude but merely a personal right, nor the act of using itself without any right, can be constituted or had in things consumed by use, since each of these requires that from the thing itself, its substance preserved, some benefit can come to the one who has the right of using, or to the one who uses; which cannot be found in things consumed by use.
units.note: The distinctions are those of Roman law: usufruct (ususfructus) and use (usus) are personal servitudes protected by real actions; the 'right of using' (ius utendi) is a merely personal right; the 'act of using' (actus utendi) is a fact. The Franciscans claimed only the last. The pope's point: all three presuppose a thing that survives its use.

units.orig: Nec obviat supradictis, quod idem praedecessor noster in ordinatione praedicta etiam illorum, quae ad vitae sustentationem pertinent, sibi et Romanae ecclesiae dominium reservarit. Hoc enim de rebus illis duntaxat debet intelligi, quae usu non sunt consumptibiles, sine quibus humana vita non est sustentabilis, quae utique non sunt pauca. Licet autem in rebus usu consumptibilibus nec ius utendi, nec ipsum uti possit constitui vel haberi: ipsis tamen poterit ius abuti. Abuti autem, dum tractatur de rebus usu consumptibilibus, pro rei consumptione sumitur, quod ei opponitur, quod est uti. Uti quidem praesupponit, quod cum usu salva rei substantia maneat; sed abuti exigit, quod cum actu huiusmodi rei substantia consumatur; quum abuti nihil aliud, quam contra naturam usus uti in hac materia proprie possit dici. Licet autem quis re usibili absque iure utendi aliquo uti possit: ipsum tamen uti etiam in re tali absque iure utendi, separato a dominio vel coniuncto, nec ab aliquo potest constitui, nec a quoquam haberi. Et quod talis usus constitui nequeat, ex hoc patet, quod dare vel constituere quod suum non est, nec ad se pertinet, nemo potest, licet interdum illud dare possit aliter, quam sit suum. Actus autem ipse utendi ad utendum pertinet, in quantum quis suorum actuum per liberum arbitrium et voluntatem dominus dicitur, quum per hoc illos non exercere valeat, vel etiam exercere. Non autem actus ipse utendi ad eum pertinet, qui concedit alii, quod in re sua actum illum valeat exercere. Quod utique nihil est aliud, quam quod actum suum ad rem concedentis ad actum suum utens valeat applicare. Sicut, qui equum suum alicui commodat, non actum equitandi concedit commodatario, sed quod actum illum in equo suo valeat exercere. Quod non est utique actum utendi simplicem concedere sine iure, quum haec concedere nihil sit aliud, quam concedere ius utendi; quod quidem ius utendi, separatum a proprietate seu dominio in rebus, quae usu consumuntur, nequit constitui, ut patet manifestius ex praedictis.
units.en: Nor does it stand against the foregoing that our predecessor in the said ordinance reserved to himself and the Roman Church the ownership also of the things that pertain to the sustenance of life. For this must be understood only of those things that are not consumed by use, without which human life cannot be sustained, and which are certainly not few. And although in things consumed by use neither the right of using nor using itself can be constituted or had, there can yet be in them a right of 'abusing'. 'Abusing', when things consumed by use are treated, is taken for the consumption of the thing, which is opposed to using. Using presupposes that the substance of the thing remains with the use; abusing requires that the substance of the thing be consumed with the act; so that in this matter abusing can properly be called nothing but using against the nature of use. And although someone may use a usable thing without any right of using, yet using itself, even in such a thing, without a right of using, separated from ownership or joined to it, can neither be constituted by anyone nor had by anyone. That such a use cannot be constituted is clear from this: no one can give or constitute what is not his and does not belong to him, though he may sometimes give it otherwise than as his own. The act of using belongs to the one using, in so far as a man is called the master (dominus) of his acts by free will and choice, since by this he can refrain from them or perform them. But the act of using does not belong to the one who grants another the right to perform that act in his thing. This is nothing but that the user may apply his own act to the thing of the grantor. So the man who lends his horse to someone does not grant the borrower the act of riding, but that he may perform that act on his horse. And this is certainly not to grant a simple act of using without right, since to grant this is nothing but to grant a right of using; and a right of using separated from property or ownership cannot be constituted in things consumed by use, as is clearer still from what has been said.
units.note: 'Abuse' (abusus) is the Roman-law term for consumption, not misuse. The example of the horse is the pope's answer to the friars' claim that a benefactor could give them a bare 'use of fact' while keeping ownership: what the owner gives is always a right.

units.orig: Praeterea quod simplex usus, id est, sine iure utendi, a proprietate seu dominio separatus, etiam in re usibili haberi nequeat, sic probatur. Si enim possit haberi usus talis, aut ante actum ipsum, aut in ipso actu, aut post completum actum huiusmodi haberetur. Quod autem hoc nequeat fieri, ex hoc patet: quod non est nequaquam haberi potest. Patet autem, quod actus ipse, antequam exerceatur, aut etiam dum exercetur, aut postquam perfectus est, in rerum natura non est: ex quo sequitur, quod haberi minime potest. Licet enim et ante actum ipsum quis facultatem illam habeat exercendi: per hoc tamen actus ipse in rerum natura, nisi in potentia, non exsistit. Quum autem actus est in fieri: nec adhuc, quod ipse actus in rerum natura sit, potest dici, licet pro eo, quod sit in fieri, dici possit. Quod enim de actu, qui est in fieri, praeteriit vel futurum est, iam non est in rerum natura, sed in memoria vel apprehensione tantum est; quare, nisi prout in memoria vel apprehensione tantum est, haberi nequaquam potest. Quod autem in praesenti fit, momentaneum vel instantaneum est, quod utique magis intellectu quam sensu percipi potest. Unde nec potest haberi pro tunc, nisi pro momento illo seu instanti, in quo quum fit, potest dici actum post actum completum. Licet, si ex facto ipso producta res aliqua fuerit, res ipsa aliqua facta haberi valeat, factum tamen ipsum, quod iam transit, nisi in memoria, (prout supra dictum est,) non habetur.
units.en: Moreover, that a simple use, that is, one without a right of using, separated from property or ownership, cannot be had even in a usable thing is proved thus. If such a use could be had, it would be had either before the act, or in the act, or after the act is completed. That this cannot be is clear from this: what does not exist can by no means be had. And it is clear that the act, before it is performed, or while it is being performed, or after it is completed, does not exist in the nature of things; from which it follows that it can by no means be had. For although before the act someone may have the faculty of performing it, the act does not by this exist in the nature of things, except potentially. And when the act is in the doing, it still cannot be said that the act is in the nature of things, though it can be said to be in the doing. For what of an act in the doing is past or future is no longer in the nature of things, but only in memory or apprehension; so that it can by no means be had except as it is in memory or apprehension. And what is done in the present is momentary or instantaneous, which can be perceived by the intellect rather than by the senses; so that it cannot be had even then, except for that moment or instant in which, while it is done, it can be called done after the completed act. Although, if some thing has been produced by the deed, that thing can be had as made, yet the deed itself, which has passed, is not had except in memory (as said above).
units.note: Scholastic metaphysics in a decretal: an act (actus) has no enduring existence, so it cannot be 'had' (haberi) as property or use are had. William of Ockham later answered at length that the friars never claimed to 'have' an act, only to use.

units.titel: An unjust use would not be perfect
units.orig: Praeterea si simplex usus absque iure utendi haberi possit ab aliquo: constat, quod non iustus esset actus utendi huiusmodi reputandus, quum ille usus fuerit, cui ius non competebat utendi. Talis autem usus non iustus ad perfectionis statum nequaquam pertinet, nec perfectioni aliquid adiicit, sed sibi repugnare potius ac detrahere noscitur manifeste. Quod autem usum non iustum conditor canonis fratribus ipsis intellexerit reservare, nequaquam debet aliquis sapiens aestimare; immo, quod de iusto intellexerit, ex eo potest evidentius apparere, quod in eadem ordinatione curavit adiicere, quod illarum rerum duntaxat in se et ecclesiam Romanam recipiebat dominium, quarum usum facti liceret habere fratribus seu ordini ante dictis, subiungens nihilominus, quod non rerum omnium usum habere debeant fratres ipsi. Quantum autem ad usum facti simplicem absque omni iure utendi attinet: nulla rerum quoad fratres differentia est censenda. Sic enim uti de facto possunt prohibitis, ut permissis. Quare praemissa rerum distinctio ad illum usum facti potius est referenda, pro quo ipsis competit fratribus ius utendi. Quarundam enim rerum usus fratribus ipsis prohibitus noscitur, et quarundam permissus. Ex quo sequitur, quod usus facti, de quo ordinatio loquitur, de tali intelligi debeat, qui iustus sit, id est, pro quo competat ius utendi. Et hoc conditor ipse canonis exprimit evidenter, quum in eadem ordinatione adiecerit, quod moderatus usus in expressis prius rebus ipsis fratribus est concessus. Praeterea si in rebus consumptibilibus possit usus constitui vel haberi: nequaquam simplex, nec a rei substantia, proprietate, seu dominio separatus usus huiusmodi posset dici, quum per talem usum, id est utendi actum, et in ipso actu, et cum ipso actu res consumatur huiusmodi, ac in ipsius rei exerceatur substantia, nec sine rei ipsius consumptione esse valeat usus talis. Ex quo patet, quod usus talis nec simplex, nec separatus a dominio potest dici.
units.en: Further, if a simple use without a right of using could be had by anyone, it is certain that such an act of using would have to be reckoned unjust, since the one who used had no right to use. But such an unjust use in no way belongs to the state of perfection, nor adds anything to perfection, but is clearly known rather to be contrary to it and to detract from it. That the maker of the canon meant to reserve an unjust use to the friars no wise man should think; rather, that he meant a just one can appear more clearly from this, that in the same ordinance he took care to add that he received into his own ownership and that of the Roman Church only those things whose use of fact the friars or the order might have, adding nevertheless that the friars ought not to have the use of all things. But as far as a simple use of fact without any right of using is concerned, no difference between things can be made as regards the friars; for they can use forbidden things in fact as well as permitted ones. Therefore that distinction of things must rather be referred to the use of fact for which the friars have a right of using. For the use of some things is known to be forbidden to the friars, and of others permitted. From which it follows that the use of fact of which the ordinance speaks must be understood of such a use as is just, that is, for which a right of using lies. And the maker of the canon expresses this clearly when he added in the same ordinance that a moderate use of the things expressly named before was granted to the friars. Moreover, if a use could be constituted or had in consumable things, such a use could by no means be called simple, nor separated from the substance, property or ownership of the thing, since by such a use, that is, by the act of using, both in the act and with the act, the thing is consumed and the act is exercised on the thing's very substance, and such a use cannot exist without the consumption of the thing. From which it is clear that such a use can be called neither simple nor separated from ownership.
units.note: The argument that a use without right would be an 'unjust use' was to become the core of Quum inter nonnullos (1323): to say that Christ used things without any right would make Christ's use unjust (Decr. Nonnullos [2]; Decr. Quorundam [4]).

units.titel: The Church in the lower courts
units.orig: Rursus nedum fratribus ipsis ordinatio praedicta non profuit, sed etiam occasionaliter honori sacrosanctae Romanae ecclesiae non leviter detrahit et detraxit. Numquid non praefatae ecclesiae derogatur honori, si ipsam oporteat nunc in foro ecclesiastico, nunc in saeculari, interdum quoque coram pedaneis iudicibus, et plerumque pro rebus parvis et vilibus continue litigare? Hoc autem notum est fieri, quum occasione retentionis dicti dominii omnes causae occurrentes agendo vel defendendo pro bonis huiusmodi nomine Romanae ecclesiae virtute cuiusdam privilegii, a felicis recordationis Martino Papa IV. praedecessore nostro concessi, super hoc agitentur, et, (quod gravius est censendum,) procuratores causarum huiusmodi multos vexare dicuntur indebite; licet potestas attributa procuratoribus talibus per privilegium ante dictum quoad administrationem bonorum praemissorum dudum servata non fuerit, nec servetur, quae omnia in notam et iniuriam sanctae Romanae ecclesiae non est dubium redundare. Adhuc ordinatio ante dicta ecclesiarum praelatis et rectoribus gravis exsistere nimium et molesta monstratur. Numquid non grave praemissis potest exsistere, quod ipsos oporteat se opponere sanctae Romanae ecclesiae, quae ipsorum caput noscitur et magistra, ac cum ea agendo vel defendendo litigare assidue, vel cedere iuri suo? Hoc tamen oportet illos facere, quum in multis dicti fratres praedictis exsistere dicantur iniurii, sicut multorum praelatorum et rectorum diversarum provinciarum adhuc in curia exsistentium habet insinuatio, qui quidem fratres facta sua per procuratores nituntur defendere ante dictos.
units.en: Again, the said ordinance not only did not benefit the friars, but also, as an occasion, detracts and has detracted not a little from the honour of the holy Roman Church. Is it not derogatory to the honour of that Church if it must continually litigate, now in the church court, now in the secular one, sometimes even before petty judges, and mostly for small and cheap things? Yet this is known to happen, since by reason of the retention of that ownership all cases that occur, in suing or defending for such goods, are conducted in the name of the Roman Church by virtue of a privilege granted by our predecessor Pope Martin IV of happy memory; and (what is to be thought graver) the procurators of such cases are said to harass many unduly; although the power given to such procurators by that privilege as to the administration of the said goods has long not been kept, nor is it kept; all of which undoubtedly redounds to the disgrace and injury of the holy Roman Church. Further, the said ordinance is shown to be very burdensome and troublesome to the prelates and rectors of churches. Is it not grievous to them that they must oppose the holy Roman Church, which is known to be their head and teacher, and litigate with it constantly, suing or defending, or give up their right? Yet they must do so, since in many matters the friars are said to wrong them, as the representation of many prelates and rectors of various provinces still present at the curia states; and the friars try to defend their deeds through the said procurators.
units.note: Martin IV's bull Exultantes in Domino (1283) had let the order name its own procurators to act for the Roman Church. The quarrels of the friars with the parish clergy over burials, confessions and bequests were old; here they become an argument of the pope's.

units.titel: The decree: the Church renounces the ownership
units.orig: Nos itaque, qui veritatem tenemur colere, velut ille, qui illius, qui veritas noscitur, licet immeriti, vicem teneamus in terris, illa volentes in sancta Dei ecclesia, quae non verbo obtinent tantum, sed quae re potius, observari, praemissis in scrutinio rectae considerationis adductis, ac deliberatione cum fratribus nostris et multis aliis praehabita diligenti, dignum arbitrantes et congruum, professores dicti ordinis non verbis tantum, non simulatis actibus, sed operibus claris, veritate suffultis, perfectioris status ac altioris paupertatis sibi praerogativam prae aliis mendicantibus vindicare, ac nihilominus honori sacrosanctae Romanae ecclesiae, (cuius obnubilari posset gloria, si tam perversae simulationi, quae profecto et ipsis simulantibus officit, et aliis scandali materiam subministrat; dissimulando illi occurrere consentiret,) ac insuper volentes indemnitati praelatorum et rectorum salubriter super hoc providere, nolentes in posterum sub praetextu seu pallio talis dominii temporalis, verbalis, nudi ac aenigmatici, tanta bona, quanta dicti fratres faciunt, infici, ac fomentum tantis malis, quanta procedunt ex simulatione huiusmodi, ministrare, de fratrum nostrorum consilio hoc edicto in perpetuum valituro sancimus, quod in bonis, quae in posterum conferentur vel offerentur, aut alias quomodolibet obvenire continget fratribus seu ordini supra dictis, (exceptis ecclesiis, oratoriis, officinis et habitationibus, ac vasis, libris et vestimentis divinis officiis dedicatis vel dedicandis, quae ad ipsos obvenient in futurum, ad quae se non extendunt adeo inconvenientia supra dicta, propter quod constitutionem istam ad illa extendi nolumus,) nullum ius seu dominium aliquod occasione ordinationis praedictae seu cuiusvis alterius, a quocunque praedecessorum nostrorum super hoc specialiter editae, Romanae ecclesiae acquiratur, sed quoad hoc habeantur prorsus ordinationes huiusmodi pro non factis. Per hoc autem in his, quae absque dictis ordinationibus in bonis praedictis ad dictam ecclesiam provenire vel pertinere quomodolibet poterant vel debebant, nullum eidem parari praeiudicium volumus, sed illa sibi expressius intacta et inviolata servamus.
units.en: We therefore, who are bound to cultivate the truth, as one who, however unworthy, holds on earth the place of him who is known to be the truth, wishing that in the holy Church of God those things be observed which hold not in word only but rather in fact; having brought the foregoing to the scrutiny of right consideration, and after diligent deliberation with our brothers and many others; judging it worthy and fitting that the professors of the said order should claim for themselves the prerogative of a more perfect state and a higher poverty than the other mendicants not by words only, not by feigned acts, but by clear works grounded in truth; and wishing also to provide soundly for the honour of the holy Roman Church (whose glory could be clouded if it consented, by dissembling, to meet so perverse a pretence, which both harms those who pretend and gives others matter for scandal), and for the indemnity of prelates and rectors; not wishing in future that such great goods as the friars do should be infected under the pretext or cloak of such a temporal ownership, verbal, bare and enigmatic, nor to feed the great evils that proceed from such a pretence: on the advice of our brothers we ordain by this edict, to be valid for ever, that in goods which in future are conferred or offered, or otherwise in any way come to the friars or the order (except churches, oratories, workshops and dwellings, and vessels, books and vestments dedicated or to be dedicated to divine service that come to them in future, to which the inconveniences mentioned do not extend so far, for which reason we do not wish this constitution to extend to them), no right or ownership whatever shall be acquired by the Roman Church by reason of the said ordinance or any other issued specially on this by any of our predecessors, but that in this respect such ordinances be held as not made. By this, however, we will that no prejudice be done to the Church in what it could or should acquire or have in those goods apart from the said ordinances; these we keep expressly untouched and inviolate for it.
units.note: 'Verbal, bare and enigmatic': the pope's description of the ownership the Roman Church had held for the friars since 1279. From now on, what was given to the friars (bread, money, land) would belong to someone, and since it no longer belonged to the Church, it belonged to the friars or to the donors: the Franciscans were made owners against their will. Churches, houses and liturgical books were excepted.

units.orig: Et quia praefatum Martini Papae praedecessoris nostri privilegium dudum servatum quoad administrationem bonorum praemissorum non exstitit, nec servatur, ac ipsorum procuratorum officium, qui nominantur a ministris et custodibus dicti ordinis, ecclesiae Romanae iniuriosum, ac multis aliis molestum noscitur et etiam onerosum: districtius inhibemus, ne deinceps pro recipiendis, petendis, extorquendis, defendendis seu administrandis bonis, quae in posterum fratribus vel ordini praedictis offerri vel conferri, seu alias obvenire continget, quisquam nominetur a quoquam seu constituatur a modo nomine sanctae Romanae ecclesiae procurator, nec occasione cuiusvis privilegii quicunque administrationem quorumcunque bonorum, quae obvenire fratribus ipsis vel ordini continget in posterum, in iudicio vel extra, agendo vel defendendo, supplicando vel alias quomodolibet assumere vel exercere dictae ecclesiae nomine audeat, nisi de sedis apostolicae licentia speciali, decernentes irritum et inane, si secus a quoquam in posterum contigerit attentari, non obstantibus quibuscunque privilegiis, a Martino Papa praedicto vel aliis praedecessoribus nostris ipsis fratribus vel ordini sub quacunque forma vel expressione verborum concessis. Per hoc autem dicti ordinis regulae in aliquo non intendimus derogare, nec privilegiis fratribus ipsis seu eorum ordini ab apostolica sede concessis, (nisi duntaxat quoad praemissa et ista tangentia,) praeiudicium aliquod generare. Nulli ergo hominum liceat hanc paginam nostrae sanctionis, inhibitionis, constitutionis et intentionis infringere, vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis autem hoc attentare praesumpserit etc. Datum Avinion. VI. Idus Decembr. Pont. nostri Ao. VII. [1322.]
units.en: And since the privilege of Pope Martin our predecessor has long not been kept as to the administration of the said goods, nor is it kept, and the office of the procurators, who are named by the ministers and custodians of the order, is known to be injurious to the Roman Church and troublesome and burdensome to many others: we strictly forbid that henceforth anyone be named by anyone, or appointed from now on, as procurator in the name of the holy Roman Church for receiving, claiming, extorting, defending or administering goods that in future are offered or conferred, or otherwise come, to the friars or the order; and that anyone by reason of any privilege dare to take on or exercise in the name of the said Church, in court or out of it, suing or defending, petitioning or in any other way, the administration of any goods that come to the friars or the order in future, except by special licence of the apostolic see; declaring void and null whatever anyone attempts otherwise in future, notwithstanding any privileges granted to the friars or the order by Pope Martin or other predecessors of ours in whatever form or expression of words. By this, however, we do not intend to derogate in anything from the rule of the order, nor to prejudice the privileges granted to the friars or their order by the apostolic see (except only as regards the foregoing and what touches it). Let no man, then, infringe this page of our sanction, prohibition, constitution and intention, or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, etc. Given at Avignon on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the seventh year of our pontificate [1322].
units.note: 8 December 1322. The Franciscan procurator general Bonagratia of Bergamo protested against this decretal in consistory on 14 January 1323 and was imprisoned; the pope then issued the revised version printed here.

sections.blurb: Two sentences that made the Franciscan doctrine a heresy: that Christ and the apostles had nothing 'individually, nor even in common', and that they had no right of using what they had.

units.orig: Quum inter nonnullos viros scholasticos saepe contingat in dubium revocari, utrum pertinaciter affirmare, Redemptorem nostrum ac Dominum Iesum Christum eiusque Apostolos in speciali non habuisse aliqua, nec in communi etiam, haereticum sit censendum, diversa et adversa etiam sentientibus circa illud: nos, huic concertationi finem imponere cupientes, assertionem huiusmodi pertinacem, quum scripturae sacrae, quae in plerisque locis ipsos nonnulla habuisse asserit, contradicat expresse, ipsamque scripturam sacram, per quam utique fidei orthodoxae probantur articuli quoad praemissa fermentum aperte supponat continere mendacii, ac per consequens, quantum in ea est, eius in totum fidem evacuans, fidem catholicam reddat, eius probationem adimens, dubiam et incertam, deinceps erroneam fore censendam et haereticam, de fratrum nostrorum consilio hoc perpetuo declaramus edicto.
units.en: Since it often happens among some scholars that it is called in question whether it is to be judged heretical to affirm pertinaciously that our Redeemer and Lord Jesus Christ and his apostles had nothing individually, nor even in common (in speciali non habuisse aliqua, nec in communi etiam), those who hold on this point views that are different and even opposed: we, desiring to put an end to this dispute, declare by this perpetual edict, on the advice of our brothers, that such a pertinacious assertion is henceforth to be judged erroneous and heretical, since it expressly contradicts sacred scripture, which in many places asserts that they had some things; and since it openly supposes that sacred scripture itself, by which the articles of the orthodox faith are proved, contains in this matter the leaven of falsehood, and so, as far as in it lies, empties scripture of all its credibility and makes the catholic faith, by taking away its proof, doubtful and uncertain.
units.note: Dated 12 November 1323. The medieval summary printed before it: 'The opinion that asserts that Christ and his disciples had nothing, and that in what they had they had no right, is erroneous and heretical. This extravagant is very notable, and has profound glosses drawn from the springs of sacred scripture.' The words condemned are almost those of the Franciscan general chapter at Perugia (June 1322): that Christ and the apostles, showing the way of perfection, had nothing 'in speciali vel in communi' by right of property or ownership. The scriptural 'places' were above all the purse that Judas carried (John 12:6; 13:29) and the common life of the first Christians (Acts 2 and 4). 'Pertinaciously' is the canonists' mark of heresy: an error held against correction. This companion game's title is taken from this sentence.

units.orig: Rursus in posterum pertinaciter affirmare, quod Redemptori nostro praedicto eius Apostolis iis, quae ipsos habuisse scriptura sacra testatur, nequaquam ius ipsis utendi competierit, nec illa vendendi seu donandi ius habuerint, aut ex ipsis alia acquirendi, quae tamen ipsos de praemissis fecisse scriptura sacra testatur, seu ipsos potuisse facere supponit expresse, quum talis assertio ipsorum usum et gesta evidenter includat, in praemissis non iusta, quod utique de usu, gestis seu factis Redemptoris nostri Dei Filii sentire nefas est, sacrae scripturae contrarium et doctrinae catholicae inimicum, assertionem ipsam pertinacem de fratrum nostrorum consilio deinceps erroneam fore censendam merito ac haereticam declaramus. Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat hanc paginam nostrarum declarationum infringere, vel ausu ei temerario contraire. Si quis autem etc. Datum Avinion. II. Idus Novembr. Ao. VII. [1323.]
units.en: Again, to affirm pertinaciously in future that our said Redeemer and his apostles had in no way a right of using the things that sacred scripture testifies they had, nor a right of selling or giving them, or of acquiring other things with them, which scripture nevertheless testifies they did with them, or expressly supposes they could do, since such an assertion plainly implies that their use and deeds in these things were not just, which it is wicked to think of the use, deeds or acts of our Redeemer, the Son of God, and is contrary to sacred scripture and hostile to catholic doctrine: this pertinacious assertion we rightly declare, on the advice of our brothers, to be henceforth judged erroneous and heretical. Let no man at all, then, infringe this page of our declarations or rashly oppose it. If anyone, etc. Given at Avignon on the second day before the Ides of November, in the seventh year [1323].
units.note: The second clause draws the consequence of Ad conditorem (Decr. Conditorem [9]): a use without right is an unjust use, and Christ's use cannot have been unjust. Friedberg prints 'Ao. VII.'; his apparatus gives VIII from the original and three manuscripts, which fits November 1323 (John XXII's eighth year began on 5 September 1323).

sections.blurb: The answer to the friars' last argument: what one pope has defined by the 'key of knowledge' another may not revoke. John XXII calls it the doctrine of the father of lies, and declares its defenders heretics and rebels. Excerpts: the opening, the friars' argument, the pope's thesis and the closing sentence.

units.orig: Quia quorundam mentes sic pater mendacii dicitur excaecasse, quod nostris constitutionibus, quarum una incipit: „Ad conditorem canonum,“ alio vero: „Quum inter nonnullos,“ utique tam cum fratribus nostris sanctae Romanae ecclesiae cardinalibus, quam cum multis archiepiscopis et episcopis, aliisque ecclesiarum praelatis, nec non et compluribus sacrae theologiae magistris, ac utriusque iuris professoribus deliberatione praehabita diligenti digestis, ac de praemissorum fratrum nostrorum consilio promulgatis, non absque multa temeritate plectibili nisi sunt detrahere, et nituntur veritatem, quam continent, per falsas insanias obfuscare: nos tam perniciosis ausibus, ne eorum doctrina pestifera simplicium animos labefacere, ac in sui erroris devium deducere valeat de eorundem fratrum consilio decernimus super hoc salubriter, (ut sequitur,) providere.
units.en: Since the father of lies is said to have so blinded the minds of certain men that they have tried, not without much punishable rashness, to disparage our constitutions, one of which begins 'Ad conditorem canonum' and the other 'Quum inter nonnullos', drawn up after diligent deliberation with our brothers the cardinals of the holy Roman Church and with many archbishops, bishops and other prelates of churches, and many masters of sacred theology and professors of both laws, and promulgated on the advice of those brothers of ours; and strive to obscure the truth they contain with false follies: we decree, on the advice of the same brothers, to provide soundly against such pernicious attempts (as follows), lest their pestilent doctrine shake the minds of simple people and lead them into the byway of their error.
units.note: Dated 10 November 1324. The medieval summary printed before it: the opinion of the detractors who presume to attack Ad conditorem and Quum inter nonnullos is reproved; after answers to all their objections they are finally declared heretics and rebels against the Roman Church, to be avoided by all, if henceforth they knowingly presume to defend or approve anything against these constitutions by word or writing; 'here, in the second and third parts, there is a long and useful disputation on the matter of the keys'. The 'certain men' included the emperor Louis the Bavarian, whose appeal of Sachsenhausen (May 1324) had called the pope a heretic for these very constitutions.

units.orig: Ad impugnandas autem constitutiones praedictas subscripta ratione tam verbo quam scripto usi sunt publice, sicut fertur. Illud, inquiunt, quod per clavem scientiae, in fide ac moribus semel diffinierunt Romani Pontifices, adeo immutabile perseverat, quod illud successori revocare non licet in dubium, nec contrarium affirmare, licet de iis, quae per clavem potestatis ordinaverint, asserant secus esse.
